summary: Specifies how to add CAST-128 to the S/MIME Cryptographic Message Syntax as an additional symmetric encryption algorithm.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds one more scrambling method to the secure email toolbox.

questions: how to use cast-128 with s/mime
what key sizes does cast-128 support
subtitle: How to plug the CAST-128 cipher into S/MIME's Cryptographic Message Syntax for content and key encryption.

tldr.problem: S/MIME requires triple-DES, which some environments find too slow, and it allows extra algorithms only if someone defines how to use them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two object identifiers for CAST-128, one for content encryption in CBC mode and one for key wrapping, plus their parameters and S/MIME client rules.
tldr.outcome: A CMS agent can now choose CAST-128, a well-studied cipher with key sizes from 40 to 128 bits, as an optional alternative to 3DES.

today: RFC 2984 is a Proposed Standard from October 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Add CAST-128
sections.content:
S/MIME is a set of specifications for the secure transport of MIME objects. In the S/MIME v3 specifications the mandatory-to-implement symmetric algorithm for content encryption and key encryption is triple-DES (3DES). The RFC says 3DES is generally considered highly secure, but that for some environments it may be seen as too slow.

S/MIME therefore allows any number of optional extra algorithms. The RFC argues that CAST-128 (defined in RFC 2144) is a suitable one: it is a well-studied symmetric cipher with relatively high performance and a variable key size from 40 bits to 128 bits. The RFC also states it is available royalty-free and license-free for commercial and non-commercial uses worldwide.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual lock for secure email can feel slow, like a very heavy door. This memo says a lighter lock called CAST-128 may be used too.

sections.title: Object Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
CAST-128 is added to the optional symmetric algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 2630) by giving it two unique object identifiers (OIDs). One names the content encryption algorithm and the other names the key encryption algorithm. A CMS agent picks the matching OID and supplies the required parameter.

For content encryption, CAST-128 in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode is RECOMMENDED, with a key length from 40 to 128 bits in 1-octet increments. The OID is cast5CBC, and its parameter holds the initialization vector iv (an octet string, default 0) and the keyLength in bits. Comments on using the IV are in RFC 2144.

For key encryption, the OID is cast5CMSkeywrap. Its parameter is only the key length as an integer, because the key wrapping procedure itself defines how and when an IV is used. Generating and distributing key-encryption keys is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each method gets its own name tag, a long number, so the two sides know which lock is in use. The tag also says how long the key is.

sections.title: Key Wrapping and Unwrapping
sections.content:
Wrapping means encrypting a content-encryption key with a key-encryption key. CAST-128 key wrapping is identical to the procedure in RFC 2630, Sections 12.6.1 and 12.6.4, with "RC2" replaced by "CAST-128" in the introduction to 12.6.4. Unwrapping follows Sections 12.6.1 and 12.6.5 in the same way.

Only 128-bit CAST-128 keys may be used as key-encryption keys, and they MUST be used with the cast5CMSkeywrapParameter set to 128. The RFC RECOMMENDS that the content-encryption key and the key-encryption key be the same size, since the content is only as secure as the smaller of the two.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping is putting one small key inside a locked box that needs a bigger key to open. The memo says the big key must be the strongest size, 128 bits.

sections.title: Using CAST-128 in S/MIME Clients
sections.content:
An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the algorithms it supports with the S/MIME capabilities attribute, which MUST be signed by the client. The OIDs SHOULD be grouped by function and MUST be listed in order of preference. A client that supports CAST-128 symmetric encryption MUST include the cast5CBC OID in the symmetric algorithms category, and MUST use the OID's parameter to show the supported key length.

For a 128-bit key, the SMIMECapability sequence MUST be DER-encoded as the hexadecimal string 301106092A864886F67D07420A300402020080.

When a sender chooses an algorithm, it weighs the capabilities lists in messages from the recipient along with private agreements, user preferences and legal restrictions. If users require CAST-128, both the sending and receiving clients MUST support it, and it MUST be set in the user preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail programs tell each other which locks they know, in order of favorite. Both sides must know CAST-128 before it can be used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CAST-128 allows variable key lengths, but the RFC warns that smaller sizes such as 40, 56 or 64 bits may be unacceptably weak for some environments. Larger sizes, such as 128 bits, are always RECOMMENDED when import, export or other laws permit.

It also repeats that the content-encryption key and the key-encryption key should be the same size, because the security of the content is at most the smaller of the two values.
sections.plainLanguage: A short key is like a flimsy padlock. Use the longest key you are allowed to, and match the key sizes on both layers.
